entities.name: Pyramid of Khafre
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Pyramid of Khafre, also known as the Pyramid of Chephren, stands as the second tallest and second largest of the three Great Pyramids of Giza, Egypt, constructed around 2570 BC during the Fourth Dynasty of the Old Kingdom. This monumental structure, originally reaching approximately 143.5 meters in height, reflects not only the architectural ingenuity of ancient Egyptians but also their religious beliefs and social hierarchies. It is widely regarded as a testament to Pharaoh Khafre's power and the central role of monumental architecture in asserting royal authority in ancient Egypt.

Constructed using an estimated 2.5 million limestone blocks, the pyramid's design features a complex internal structure, including a burial chamber and various passageways. Unlike its neighboring pyramids, it retains some of its original casing stones at the apex, showcasing the advanced stoneworking techniques of the period. The Pyramid of Khafre was part of a larger funerary complex that included a mortuary temple and the famous Great Sphinx, which is believed to bear the likeness of Khafre himself. This grand undertaking required vast resources and labor, illustrating the organizational capabilities of the ancient Egyptian state.

The legacy of the Pyramid of Khafre extends far beyond its immediate historical context; it has influenced countless generations, serving as a symbol of ancient Egyptian civilization. The pyramid's design has been studied and revered, inspiring modern architecture and continuing to attract tourists and scholars alike. Its enduring presence on the Giza plateau has made it a focal point for discussions on ancient engineering, religion, and the socio-political dynamics of the time. The artistry and scale of Khafre's pyramid exemplify the achievements of a society that placed immense value on the afterlife and the divine right of kings.
